big: A client needs money in 6 months. There are more than a dozen SEBI debt fund categories on offer, and most of them are sorted by one number: duration. Pick the wrong band and a price swing can eat the interest.

lines: Which debt fund category suits money I need in 6 months?
First see how SEBI lines up the categories by duration. Then we match the band to your date.

small: Top of each band, in months
alt: Bars of the longest duration each SEBI debt fund category may have, in months
caps: SEBI sorts most debt funds by duration. Overnight funds hold securities maturing in 1 day.
Liquid funds hold up to 91 days. Ultra short has a duration of 3 to 6 months, and low duration 6 to 12.
Money market funds hold instruments up to 1 year. Short duration is 1 to 3 years, medium 3 to 4.
Medium to long runs to 7 years, and long duration is above 7. Bars show the top of each band, in months.

alt: Four fund categories with the minimum each must hold and the part left to the manager
caps: Gilt funds must hold at least 80% in government securities.
Corporate bond funds: at least 80% in AA+ and above.
Credit risk funds: at least 65% in AA and below.
Banking and PSU funds: at least 80% in banks, PSUs and public financial institutions.
Striped parts are the manager's choice. Read the category and the scheme document.

rows: Months of yield to earn it back
alt: Liquid fund against a long-duration fund: price fall for a 1% rise in yields and months of yield to recover it
caps: A long duration fund starts above 7 years of duration. A liquid fund has about 0.2 years.
Yields rise 1%: the long fund's price falls about 7%. The liquid fund's falls about 0.2%.
At assumed yields of 7.5% and 6.5%, the long fund needs about 11 months of income to earn it back.
The liquid fund needs under half a month.
A 6-month goal needs a band that recovers within the wait.

q: Rohan has a goal in 6 months and a bank balance he can set aside today. Which category fits that date best?
opts: Long duration, because a rate cut is expected within the half-year
Liquid, because the holdings mature within 91 days and swings stay tiny
Corporate bond, because AA+ and above holdings cannot lose value
Medium duration, because it still falls inside the next four years
why: Long duration needs years, not months, to average out. A single rate rise in six months could cost more than the interest.
Liquid funds hold securities up to 91 days. Their short duration keeps price swings small, so they fit money needed soon.
Credit quality is not rate risk. AA+ bonds with long maturities can still fall in price when yields rise.
Medium duration runs 3 to 4 years. A six-month goal ends long before the swings have time to average out.

q: Meena puts ₹3 lakh, needed in one year, into a gilt fund because it carries no credit risk. What has she overlooked?
opts: Gilt funds are the only debt funds that pay tax at slab rate
Gilt funds invest only in bonds that mature within a year
Gilt funds can hold long G-secs, so rate swings can be large
Gilt funds can be redeemed only after a one-year lock-in
why: Tax treatment does not depend on the gilt label alone. It depends on whether the fund counts as specified debt-oriented.
Gilt funds are not limited to one year. They can hold G-secs of any maturity, which is why they can swing a lot.
A gilt fund holds at least 80% in G-secs, with no cap on maturity. Credit is safe but long G-secs swing a lot.
Open-ended gilt funds have no lock-in. The risk is price swings from duration, not the ability to redeem.

q: A factsheet shows a fund's Macaulay duration at 3.4 years. Which SEBI category does that fit?
opts: Medium to long duration, 4 to 7 years
why: Medium duration funds have a Macaulay duration of 3 to 4 years, and 3.4 sits inside that band.
Short duration is 1 to 3 years. A duration of 3.4 years is above that band, so it does not fit.
Medium to long runs 4 to 7 years. At 3.4 years the fund is below that band.
Low duration is 6 to 12 months. A fund at 3.4 years is far above that, so it is not low duration.

q: A client's fund shows 70% in bonds rated AA and below, and the rest in AAA. Its category label is hidden. Which category's rule does that portfolio fit?
opts: Corporate bond, which needs at least 80% in AA+ and above
Banking and PSU, which needs at least 80% in banks and PSUs
Gilt, which needs at least 80% in government securities
Credit risk, which needs at least 65% in AA and below
why: A corporate bond fund holds at least 80% in AA+ and above. This portfolio has 70% in AA and below, which breaks that rule.
Banking and PSU funds hold at least 80% in banks, PSUs and public financial institutions. This portfolio is mostly lower-rated papers.
A gilt fund holds mostly government securities. Bonds rated AA and below are company bonds, so 70% of them rules gilt out.
Credit risk funds must hold at least 65% in AA and below. A 70% share meets that rule.

pts: Duration drives the category: overnight, liquid, money market, ultra short, low, short, medium, medium to long, long.
Gilt means G-secs, and credit risk means lower-rated papers. Always read the scheme document.
Match the holding period to the category's duration.
